Just need him to accept the approach to start.
Mr Donaldson.
Kia ora.
Right. Thank you. I'm Greg O'Connor, I'm the chair of the committee.
Just to introduce ourselves, to my right, I have the-
Kia ora, Brian. I'm Greg Fleming, national MP for
Maungakiekie-Tamaki-
And to my left, I have...
Kia ora. I'm Celia Wade-Brown from the Greens.
Hello. Sam Athfield, Member of Parliament for Tauranga.
All right. Now, Mr Donaldson, thank you for
coming in and giving us your time. So now we've got 10 minutes.
You can take your submission as having been read,
and hopefully you'll obviously prepare to summarize
that. I can see you've got your paper there, and leave time for questions at the
end.
Sure thing.
The airwaves are yours.
Kia ora koutou. My name is Byron. I am the caregiver
of my father. I have a lifelong disability.
I've spent years navigating MSD and NASC and the
wider disability system.
I'm also speaking for the
many disabled people and families who deal with the same issues
but don't have the energy, confidence or support to stand here today.
My petition is simple. Remove support living payment reviews
for people with lifelong disabilities.
A lifelong disability does not change, but the review process keeps treating
people as if it is might.
Number one, the core problem. The Supported Living Payment
process is unnecessary, harmful, and insignificant for
people with permanent disabilities.
There are people who already have medically certified as having
conditions that will not improve.
They already are assessed by NASC.
They are already recognized as permanently disabled by the health system.
Yet MSD continues to require periodic reviews,
sometimes every year, sometimes every two years, to check
whether their lifelong disability is still lifelong.
This makes no sense medically, practically, or ethically.
The review process creates four major harms.
Number one, stress and fear. Disabled people and their
families live with constant anxiety that a review could
disrupt or remove essential income.
Even when the review is routine, the fear is real, and for
many people, the Support Living Payment is the difference between stability
and crisis. Number two, administration burden.
People with lifelong disabilities often rely on carers,
advocates, or overstretched support workers to manage paperwork.
Reviews add unnecessary workload to people who already
struggle with fatigue, cognitive load, or health struggles.
Number three, system ineffectuality.
MSD staff spend time processing reviews that will never
result in a change. That time could be spent supporting people
whose circumstances do change.
Number four, contradictions between agencies.
NASC assessments already confirm permanent disability.
Medical specialists already confirm permanent disability.
MSD reviews ignore these certifications and
require people to reprove what has already been proven.
This is not a small inconvenience.
It is a structural flaw that causes real harm.
Number two, real-world impacts. I want to speak to the
lived reality behind this petition.
My disability is lifelong. It will not improve, it will not
change. Yet every review cycle, we go through the same
process, gathering documents, contacting doctors, waiting for
MSD responses, and hoping nothing gets lost or
misinterpreted. For me, the stress is overwhelming,
and as a caregiver, it is exhausting.
We are not alone. I've
spoken with families who dread the envelope
arriving in the mail, people who panic when
MSD calls, people who have been traumatized by past
interactions with government agencies and now have to relive that stress
every review cycle.
Some disabled people don't have advocates, some don't
have family. Some don't have the capacity to navigate
bureaucracy. A review that should be simple becomes a
barrier to sustainability, dignity, and well-being.
The system should not be creating fear for people who are already
vulnerable.
Number three, what this petition asks for.
My petition asks for a clear, practical change.
Number one is remove Support Living Payment reviews
for people with medically certified long life disabilities.
If a disability is permanent, the income support should be permanent.
Number two, create a permanent Support Living Payment
category. This would align with MSD and with
MASCC as a medical reality. Number
three, shift review by default to review
only if circumstances change. If income changes, if
living situations change, review it, but don't review the
disability itself when it is medically confirmed as lifelong.
Number four, reduce administrative flow on MSD.
This change frees staff to focus on people whose situations
generally require reassessment.
This is not a radical change. It is a correction of an outdated process.
Number four, why this change is responsible and necessary.
This change is medically sound.
Lifelong disabilities do not improve. Cost-effective.
Fewer unnecessary reviews. Ethical means
reduces harm and stress. Practical aligns
MSD and NASC and medical
certifications. Dignified respects disabled people as citizens,
not cases to be reproven. This is a small administrative
shift with a large human impact.
Here is my closing statement. In closing, I want to emphasize one
thing. People with lifelong disabilities deserve
sustainability, dignity, and freedom from unnecessary
bureaucratic stress. Removing these reviews is a simple,
compassionate, and effective change that will make real difference in people's
lives.
All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Donaldson.
And Celia Wade-Brown.

I'm briefly going to explain the types of reviews that people on the Supported

I'm focusing on the eligibility and the reviews for people

disability, and injury. Eligibility for the
Supported Living Payment is underpinned by an assessment of a person's work
capacity,
rather than just having a health condition, disability, or injury.
This is because a key purpose of the welfare system is to support
people to find and remain in employment.
A non-reviewable category of the Supported Living Payment already

process.
So,

a week in open employment.

There are some

unlikely to improve. So generally, that would be that a person
requires constant assistance from others for all aspect of their personal

At the end of March this year, there were

So I'm now going to just talk about the two types of reviews you generally
would be required to complete as part of the Supported Living Payment.
The first is medical reviews, and the second is a review called
confirming your circumstances or mandatory reviews.
So medical reviews
require people who are granted the Supported Living Payment who don't
qualify for simplified access to be reassessed every
two years to ensure they continue to meet the medical qualifications.
That is, they are both permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to
work. This review is required because a person's work
capacity may change over time, and the impact of their health
condition on their capacity to work may change over time.
It may deteriorate, or it may improve.
This is not necessarily because the person's condition has
improved or resolved, but it may be because with
support, they may be able to engage in some work preparation or
employment.
People can provide a new medical certificate for a medical review with their
health practitioner, or they may be able to provide another suitable recent
assessment as long as the assessment provides the information that
MSD can use to determine eligibility.
Using information already available from existing assessments is intended to make
that review process easier for people.
The second review is a review of circumstances, or also called mandatory
reviews, and these are done every 52 weeks.
And their purpose is to check that people are receiving the correct rate
of assistance and that they continue to be eligible.
So this review is generally confirming that the information MSD
has about people is correct, and especially those that
may impact the rate of assistance and the type of assistance.
So things like income, relationship status, whether they have dependent
children in their care. If they're receiving the accommodation supplement or the
disability allowance, we'll verify that that hasn't changed or
increased or decreased. It's a really important review to
ensure that we pay the correct rate of assistance and that people don't incur a lot
of debt through overpayment because of a change in circumstance.
And that is done annually. But we do understand that if people get into debt, that
creates a lot of distress because MSD must recover any debt or
overpaid benefits.
So people must respond to that circumstance review.
If they don't respond, their benefit can be suspended.
That, again, is to prevent debt or paying inappropriately.
These reviews are not the same as a reapplication.
Reapplications are for people who are on job seeker support or who are on a
temporary benefit who need to reapply to get that assistance.
In closing, I just want to recognize that for some people, the
experience of applying for and maintaining their
income support is very challenging.
We consider that the simplified access policy does help with that and allows
MSD under those criteria just to improve the application process
for people who have that permanent and severe condition that's never
going to change in accordance with the criteria.
But annual reviews remain a really important way for us to check in people's
circumstances and ensure that we update our information and don't overpay people.
I just want to thank you for the opportunity to respond, and I'm happy to take

That's very helpful.
Yes.

Whether,

So I am Pippa Eden-Mann. I'm the National Policy Analyst for CCS
Disability Action. We strongly support this petition.
Our central message today is simple: people with lifelong disabilities,
impairments, or health conditions should not be required to repeatedly prove a
permanent condition is still permanent in order to retain essential
income support. The supported living payment exists
primarily for people who are unable to work long-term or permanently
because of a disability, impairment, or health condition.
The threshold for receiving the support is already high.
People don't receive the supported living payment lightly.
They've already had to have gone through rigorous medical assessment and a
fairly arduous administrative process before being found
eligible. Yet even when a person's
condition has been confirmed as lifelong or permanent, they can still
be required to complete repeated reviews and
provide updated medical evidence.
For many disabled people, this is not a neutral administrative
step. It can involve cost, stress, uncertainty, and
real risk.
A person may need to book and pay for a GP appointment simply to
confirm what is already known, that their disability or health condition has
not disappeared.
For disabled people who already experience
higher rates of financial hardship, that cost is not minor.
It may mean choosing between medical paperwork and other essential living
costs. One in five disabled people cannot afford to go to the GP
when they need to.
The consequences of not completing a review can also be severe.
If a person cannot secure an appointment in time, cannot afford the
appointment, misses correspondence, or struggles to navigate the process,
their payments may be delayed, suspended, or canceled.
For people who rely on this income to meet basic needs, that risk is significant.
It is particularly concerning because the welfare system can be complex and
difficult to navigate. Many disabled people do not know about
simplified access, and many medical professionals are also unclear about
the process and what qualifies as well.
Disabled people should not be placed in a position where the continuation of
essential support depends on repeatedly
engaging with processes that are not always accessible,
user-centered, or proportionate to their circumstances.
There's also a wider systems issue. General practice is under significant pressure.
It's not a good use of scarce medical appointments for GPs to repeatedly complete
paperwork confirming that permanent conditions that
have already been assessed are still permanent.
That time could be better directed towards people who are seeking care for
acute medical health needs.
The same applies to the welfare system.
MSD staff time and public resources shouldn't be spent on reassessing
circumstances where the outcome's already known.
Repeated medical reviews of lifelong disabilities do not make the system
fairer or more effective. They create unnecessary administration
and unnecessary
harm.
And this practice is also inconsistent with a rights-based approach to
disability. It undermines a disabled person's
dignity. It tells disabled people that they must continue to justify their
existence and their need for support when their disability or
condition is permanent.
Conditions like Down syndrome, significant lifelong conditions such as
autism, or permanent loss of function don't disappear because
another two years has passed. We acknowledge that public
systems do require accountability.
However, accountability should be targeted, proportionate, and evidence-based.
It should not impose recurring burdens on people whose eligibility rests on the
conditions already confirmed as permanent and
irreversible.
For these reasons, CCS Disability Action recommends that the government end the
periodic medical reviews for supported living payment recipients with medically
confirmed permanent disabilities, impairments, or health conditions that will not
improve over time. We also recommend working with disabled people,
disability organizations, and medical professionals to
develop clear and consistent criteria for conditions, disabilities,
and impairments that should be treated as permanent and
irreversible for the purpose of review exemptions such as the
simplified access.
In addition, we are also recommending wider consultation with the disability
community about how to reduce barriers within the welfare system and
ensure that the processes are accessible and
user-centered and consistent with the dignity and rights of disabled
people. Disabled people with lifelong disabilities should not have to
repeatedly prove that they are still disabled in order to
receive the support that they need to live.
The current review requirements cause avoidable stress, impose
avoidable costs, and use public resources in ways
that don't
serve disabled people, medical professionals, or the welfare system well.
Permanent disability should be
recognized as permanent. CCS Disability Action therefore
supports the petition and urges the government to remove
supported living payment medical benefit reviews for people with lifelong and
permanent disabilities. And I'm happy to take any questions.

But

She coming through now.

Ko Debbie Hughes toku ingoa. I am the Chief Executive of the New Zealand
Disability Support Network, or NZDSN.
NZDSN is the national peak body representing disability support
providers across Aotearoa. Our members support disabled
people to live good lives, participate in their communities, and
where possible, access meaningful employment.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to our submission on Byron
Donaldson's petition concerning supported living payment
reassessments for people with lifelong disabilities.
I want to begin by acknowledging the concern at the heart of this petition.
No disabled person should be repeatedly required to prove
that they still have a permanent disability or medical
condition that will not change. This can be stressful and
demeaning for disabled people and their families, as well as
creating unnecessary administrative work.
Importantly, MSD already has a process to address
this.
Through its simplified access process, MSD can identify
people whose condition is permanent and whose
circumstances mean they should not be required to
repeatedly provide medical evidence or undergo
assessment. We support that existing approach.
Where it is clear that a person's circumstances will not
change, they should continue to be exempt from repeated
reassessment.
Our concern is therefore not with protecting people from
unnecessary reassessment. We agree with that.
Our concern is with using the broader category of
lifelong disability as the basis for
automatically exempting everyone from any future
review or discussion about employment.
There is an important difference between having a lifelong disability and
having no current or future capacity to
participate in employment. Those are not the
same thing.
Mm-hmm.
A disability may be lifelong, but its impact on a
person's life and the opportunities available to that
person can change considerably over time.
People gain skills. They complete education and training.
Their health or personal circumstances change.
New technology becomes available.
Workplaces become more accessible.
Employers become more flexible. More importantly,
people may gain access to the right support at the right time.
A diagnosis alone cannot tell us whether someone can
work.
Autism, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, intellectual
disability, blindness, and deafness are all lifelong
disabilities. But the impact on each of these
disabilities varies significantly from person to person.
Many people with lifelong disabilities are already participating
successfully in the workforce-
Mm-hmm
... sometimes independently and sometimes with ongoing support
or workplace accommodations.
If we automatically exempted everyone with a lifelong
disability from any future consideration of
employment, we would risk making a very different and
equally damaging assumption that lifelong
disability means lifelong incapacity.
Mm.
That is not consistent with the New Zealand Disability Strategy,
Enabling Good Lives, or the United Nations Convention
on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
Article 27 of the convention affirms the right of disabled people to
work on an equal basis with others.
That requires us to create genuine pathways into employment
and provide the support and reasonable accommodation people need to
succeed.
Employment is not the right outcome for every person, and
paid work should never be treated as the measure of a person's value.
Disabled people contribute to their families and communities in many different
ways.
However, when employment is possible and wanted, it can bring greater
financial independence, stronger social connection,
increased confidence, and a sense of purpose and greater choice and control.
We should be careful not to design a system that unintentionally
closes that door.
Our concern is that a blanket exemption based solely on a lifelong
diagnosis could result in people being written off too early
and potentially for the rest of their lives.
However, retaining periodic reviews is only
useful if those reviews are fair, humane, and
genuinely supportive.
A review should not simply require a disabled people to repeatedly
prove their eligibility for income support.
It should not begin from a position of suspicion or create
fear that essential financial support will be
removed. At its best, a review should be a
constructive checkpoint. It should consider whether the person's
circumstances or aspirations have changed, and whether new
services, training, technology, or workplace support
could help them pursue employment if that is what they want.
If we continue to review people but do not provide meaningful
pathways into employment, we have retained the burden,
but without delivering the benefit.
There is little value in repeatedly asking whether a person can work if
suitable employment services are unavailable,
workplaces remain inaccessible, or employers are
unwilling to provide reasonable accommodation.
The quality and purpose of the review process
therefore matter just as much as its frequency.
NZDSN's position is that MSD should retain its
existing simplified access process for people who should
not be subjected to repeated reassessment.
For other people with lifelong disabilities, some form of
proportionate periodic review may remain
appropriate.
That review should be individualized and consider the functional
impact of the person's disability, their circumstances,
their aspirations, and the support available to them.
It should not rely on diagnosis alone, and it should not assume
that eligibility for income support disappears
simply because a person may be able to undertake some work.
This is not a choice between protecting disabled people from
unnecessary reassessment and supporting disabled people into
employment. We can and should do both.
We therefore recommend that the existing exemption process
remains available to people whose circumstances clearly
warrant it. We also recommend retaining proportionate
periodic reviews for others where there may be
potential or a desire to participate in employment
now or in the future.
These decisions should be based on the individual and the functional
impact of their disability, not simply whether their
diagnosis is lifelong.
Finally, any employment-focused review must be connected to
real and adequately resourced support.
A review should open doors. It should not simply test
